item.title: When giving up teaches you more than persevering ever could
item.dc:creator: Mario I Juarez-Garcia
item.description:
Grit is all well and good, but sometimes abandoning your goals can be crucial to discovering who you are

- by Mario I Juarez-Garcia

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
After three years and more than 20 rejections, I asked myself a difficult question: should I give up? The evidence seemed clear. American universities did not want me as a philosophy graduate student. The world was telling me that an academic life was nothing more than a teenage dream. My lifelong goal of becoming a professional philosopher appeared to founder on the shoals of academia. It was time to decide whether it made sense to continue pursuing what the world told me was an unachievable project. But how does one decide when it’s time to give up?

In theory, there is a tidy formula to know when to abandon a goal: when the expected utility of quitting becomes greater than the expected utility of pursuing it. But, of course, the clean theoretical answer dissolves in the strange complexities of life. When we face the question of giving up in reality, expected utility is really just an arbitrary personal estimation. The moment for giving up is messy, determined more by one’s idiosyncratic criteria and personality than anything that could reasonably be considered objective. This opens the door to further questions: what if the next try is the successful one? Am I letting all of my past efforts go to waste? What kind of person am I if I give up?

It is especially difficult to abandon goals when we are surrounded by stories of victorious grit. Popular culture adores portrayals of unlikely success, of those who experience setbacks, keep trying, refuse to surrender, and then, despite the overwhelming odds, win. ‘Losers’ and ‘quitters’ are insults in a society that prizes those who never give up. But the value of persistence not only permeates popular culture. It has also prompted moral philosophers to stress the virtues of grit.

Philosophers have recently been animated by the challenge of grasping the nature and rationality of persistence. One important thinker about persistence was the American philosopher Robert Nozick, who held that honouring our past efforts builds a commitment that helps us overcome the temptation to quit and may push us to achieve long-term goals. In a similar line of thought, Jennifer Morton and Sarah Paul invite readers to always start long-term projects with the strong belief that they will succeed despite evidence to the contrary, which in favourable circumstances can overcome deadening inertia. Others, like Elizabeth Jackson, underline hope as fundamental for rationalising the pursuit of long-term goals despite evidence of failure and temptations to give up. Philosophers thus contribute to a culture of perseverance.

Despite its virtues, an important problem of a culture of perseverance is that it hides exactly what it denies: the positive value of giving up. Grit is all well and good, but in real life, abandoning goals is crucial to discovering who we are. This is what I call the exploratory value of giving up: quitting may reveal skills, limitations and passions that could not have been known prior to failure.

To grasp the exploratory value of giving up, we must understand the process of choosing goals. Rational choice theory distinguishes between means and goals. Goals fall beyond the purview of rationality; they are chosen according to our preferences. Once chosen, goals provide the fixed point from which the means can be rationally chosen. But mere pursuit of preference is not the only way to choose goals. They can also be selected according to the means that are available through a process of exploration and improvisation. Saras Sarasvathy, a theorist of entrepreneurship, explains these two ways of choosing goals with a mundane illustration: deciding what to have for dinner. We can choose a dish from a cookbook, buy the ingredients, follow the recipe, and voilà! This is normally how we think about pursuing goals: we choose one, develop the necessary skills, and strive to achieve it. The goal determines the means. In a culture of perseverance, any goal we choose is supposed to be achievable – and, if we fail, it is because we did not try hard enough.

What are the chances that we get the right combination of ingredients on the first try?

But there is another way to choose what to have for dinner. You can first look at the ingredients you have in the cupboard and improvise. This is a different selection process. The ingredients determine the dish. Sarasvathy holds that the second strategy is the way entrepreneurs build successful businesses: they try and fail until they figure out what they do well, and only then do they persevere. They give up on bad business ideas before choosing the right one. This framework allows us to grasp the exploratory value of giving up: we discover ‘the ingredients in our cupboard’ through our failures. Giving up is often a step toward self-knowledge.

Consider the choice of long-term goals. These goals are like unknown ingredients in the cupboard: we need to try them first to see what can be useful. What are the chances that we get the right combination of ingredients on the first try? Likewise, what are the chances that the first goal teenagers choose will fulfil them as adults? The earliest life goals one adopts are often chosen from a place of ignorance and childish illusion. But if we acknowledge that those goals are temporary and are attentive to the reasons for our failures, we are likely to gain knowledge about ourselves.

Initial goals are what the philosopher David Schmidtz, in his article ‘Choosing Ends’ (1994), calls maieutic ends, those ‘end[s] achieved through a process of coming to have other ends’. Maieutic ends are provisional and hence can orient the search for other goals. We might realise that we were not talented enough to become musicians, that we sabotage romantic relationships that feel too close to be safe, or that we do not want to spend years writing a dissertation, and so on. Being attentive to failure is being alert to one’s skills, talents and drives. The search is not easy, and it might need to restart many times throughout a lifetime, not always because the lessons are not learned, but because we change with the circumstances.

Other times what is learned from failure is not something about ourselves, but about the context of our life. An ambitious young woman from rural West Virginia realises that she lacks the means to go to college; an Indigenous writer from Chiapas who works in his mother tongue accepts that his texts will not be read by many; the chair of the literature department of a small university comes to terms with the fact that the administration is gradually eliminating the humanities. Failure helps us learn that our conditions are not right for the goal we are pursuing. Yet reality is not so malleable. When our surroundings are working against us, the right strategy is not always to change them. Sometimes it is better to change ourselves. That wisdom can be found in René Descartes’s words: ‘my … maxim was to endeavour always to conquer myself rather than fortune, and change my desires rather than the order of the world.’ Maybe that ambitious young woman from rural West Virginia must find ways to succeed that do not involve college; perhaps the writer from Chiapas needs to learn to write some texts in English; and the literature professor may need to find a way to make a living outside academia.

Consider again the original question. How do we know when one should give up? In theory, the answer is straightforward; in reality, asking for the optimal point for abandoning goals seems to be the wrong question. The right one is different: would I know myself better if I gave up? This is what ultimately helped me decide to quit trying to become an academic philosopher. I did not renew my adjunct contract at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and took over the old office job of a good friend. It wasn’t much, but it was a place to start reimagining my life. Then, after a week of taking the new job, I couldn’t tolerate how unmotivating the office job was. It was worse than the sting of rejections. So I confirmed that what moved me was doing philosophy. What I really had to give up on was the office job – and what I had to persist with was the PhD applications. For two more years I applied. The first year I was rejected. Then, one day, I was accepted at the University of Arizona. The risk paid off. But it might not have done. Giving up on philosophy might have led me to a better place. I doubt it, not because I persevered, but because, for one week, I did not. That is how I learned what moved me.

Friedrich Nietzsche’s aphorism ‘What does not kill me makes me stronger’ has become a cliché at the core of a culture of perseverance. But it implies an often overlooked truth: what does not make us stronger may also teach us who we are.

item.title: The bookshelf builder
item.dc:creator: Carey Baraka
item.description:
Ellah Wakatama is editor, agent, publisher and mentor, all rolled into one. Her mission: to put the work of gifted Black writers into the literary canon

- by Carey Baraka

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Not long ago, a group of East African writers gathered at my house in Nairobi for a writing weekend. We were all working on manuscripts – novels set in Kenya and in Kazakhstan, histories of people in Ethiopia and Uganda, works we each imagined would be our magnum opus – but the problem, invariably, was how we might turn these into published books. Over beers and pizza, we brainstormed. Maybe what we needed was to be agented in London or in New York. Maybe what we needed was to move to London or New York. Maybe we simply needed to support each other, edit one another’s manuscripts. (But how would that help us get published?) Then, a Somali author who’d won some of Africa’s most important literary prizes for shorter work, chimed in. What we needed, he said, was to be adopted by Ellah Wakatama.

To be an African writer today – especially one writing in English, especially one younger than 40 – is to reckon with the idea of Ellah. Born in Zimbabwe when it was still under the Rhodesian flag, and now based in Britain, she is an editor-at-large at Canongate, an independent publishing firm. But it is more accurate to describe her as the most powerful woman – person – in Anglophone African literature today. From friends whose books she has touched, one hears of the fury of her red pen, of what they describe as the best editing they’ve ever experienced. From those who’ve worked with her, one hears of a person who doesn’t suffer fools, nor clichés like ‘suffer fools’. No other individual has so influenced the 21st-century African canon, if there is such a thing. Wakatama calls it ‘the bookshelf that my grandchildren will refer to’. Her lifelong project is to shape that bookshelf, to turn it into a library unto itself.

The night went on, as did the weekend. We’d all laughed when he said it, but beneath our laughter were three uneasy truths:

  1. There were no publishers in East Africa who would put out our work.
  2. We were doomed to try and find our own way into publishing networks in the West.
  3. Having a literary godparent was what had worked for generations of African writers.

In the beginning was Chinua Achebe. It is a rule of African literature that any exegesis has to begin with him. Achebe is famous as a novelist – Things Fall Apart (1958) really is one of those great books that everyone should read before they die – but he was more important as an editor of Heinemann’s African Writers Series (AWS), which introduced Western readers to an array of African authors, fledgling and established alike. Novels by African writers had existed before Achebe but, for writers of a certain generation, the AWS was arguably the only publishing vehicle for their work. The great Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, for instance, had his first book published because he gave his manuscript to Achebe. Now we needed to give our manuscripts to Wakatama. She was editor, agent, publisher and godparent, all rolled into one.

But how had she become this person? How did a kid from Harare grow up to wield such influence? I, a kid from Kisumu, a city in Kenya, was determined to track how this had come to be.

The idea of Ellah is different from Ellah in person. In June 2025, I met Wakatama in Accra where she was leading a writing workshop for Pfumo, a Pan-African literary collective she’d recently co-founded. Who was this person in front of me, smoking a cigarette she’s rolled herself? So giggly, so cheery, a bit frilly. She squealed when we passed the store of her favourite Ghanaian designer. I wanted to gossip with her. She exuded fun.

I put to her my Achebe comparison, although I could already see holes: Wakatama’s hair is far more glorious and, unlike the grand old man of African letters, she’d never been a novelist, though she’d briefly tried to be a poet, and co-authored a book of short stories when she was 21. Wakatama, laughing, wouldn’t agree with the Achebe analogy – we both knew that would be in bad taste – but said she could see the throughline of my logic. She was, after all, a child of the age that the AWS represented and sought to shape: Africa after empire.

The second child of Winnie Ndoro and Pius Wakatama, Ellah spent her first four years in a village south of Harare with her grandparents. Winnie and Pius had met at work: she, educated, was a secretary; he, a township boy who sold newspapers, had, Ellah told me, very much ‘married up’. Pius didn’t finish high school but he could write in English; he’d read the short fiction in DRUM, a South African magazine he sold, and thought to himself: I can do that! He could, and did, and then became a novelist in the Shona language, well-known enough that he was invited for a residency at the University of Iowa.

‘I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia’

This time, the whole family went. In Iowa, little Ellah struggled to make friends, partly because she barely spoke English. Once, she saw a group of Black girls playing outside but they wouldn’t speak to her since all she spoke was Shona. That people who looked like her couldn’t understand her was deeply unsettling; soon after, Ellah stopped talking altogether for six months. When she resumed, she stuttered badly in English. Her mother, Winnie, enlisted a speech therapist who used C S Lewis’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe to help her. If you can read this word w-a-r-d-r-o-b-e without stuttering, the therapist once told her, we will have a peach melba. Ellah thought and thought, said the word without tripping over it, then snarfed down her reward.

Perhaps that’s where it started – the belief that books could be a salve against the world. A few years later, when her class went on a field trip to see a wardrobe that had once belonged to C S Lewis, Ellah packed spare socks, a sandwich and a flashlight because she was going to Narnia and not coming back. But when they opened it, it was just an empty wardrobe. ‘I was really disappointed,’ she told me. ‘And I feel I have been looking for Narnia ever since. Every book I open, I’m looking for Narnia.’

In 1976, the family moved back to Zimbabwe, where a war of liberation was being waged. A year before Ellah was born, the white minority in Rhodesia had seized power, declaring independence from Britain. Consequently, two liberation groups – ZANU and ZAPU – had started a resistance war, rejecting rule by a clique of white settlers. Pius and Winnie wanted to be home when it was won. Ten-year-old Ellah, no longer mute, had forgotten how to speak in Shona. Winnie enrolled her in the best private elementary school in Zimbabwe at the time. Only white girls were students at Bishopslea but Winnie saw no reason why her daughters shouldn’t get the best education. Neither did the school’s British headmistress. But the Rhodesian government was angry this had happened, and they deported the headmistress.

All the while, the war continued. Some of Ellah’s relatives were either fighting or living in villages fenced off because of the war. Her classmates were told to support their soldiers; one year, they had to knit balaclavas for the prime minister Ian Smith’s forces, so Ellah went home and asked her mother for green yarn. Winnie was furious; no daughter of hers was going to make balaclavas for the Rhodesians. Ellah cried and cried; all she wanted was to fit in with the other girls. As a compromise, Winnie bought her brown wool – nothing but the green of the Rhodesian flag would fit the Rhodesians.

‘It had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world’

This is one part of what shaped Wakatama. The memories of the war. The race laws in Zimbabwe. The fury with which her mother disregarded them while ensuring that her children were equipped to navigate them. The other part is books. Ellah moved from Nancy Drew and The Hardy Boys to Hermann Hesse and Taban Lo Liyong, working through her father’s library. She wrote Liyong a fan letter; to her delight, he responded. She and her best friend forged their mothers’ signatures so that they could borrow Georgette Heyer paperbacks from the adult library. Then, in 1980 – the year of the first free elections, of Zimbabwe’s independence, of the start of high school – she was assigned to read Doris Lessing in class.

Lessing’s The Grass Is Singing (1950) – the story of the relationship between Mary, a poor white farmer’s wife, and Moses, a Black servant on the homestead – was the first book Wakatama read that was set in Zimbabwe. She found it shocking – and confusing. ‘As a girl, I wanted to become a woman who stood at the vanguard of the battlelines that Lessing had set out, the questions she asked about selfhood and a woman’s place in the world,’ she would later say. ‘But Moses was the one who was my relative.’ It was a challenge in newly independent Zimbabwe to hold both those stories: ‘Lessing, on the one hand, speaking for my gender, and her boldly imagined Moses, on the other hand, bearing witness to my people’s dispossession.’

Enflamed by Lessing, she started writing fiction. A magazine called Moto had a monthly short-story competition, top prize $100, which she entered and won. Her story was about a prison inmate suffering an existential crisis – full of ‘deep emotion, injustice and pretty sentences’. With her prize money, she bought a pair of shoes, grey snakeskin. ‘My brother was at school with a Kenyan boy I really liked,’ she added. ‘So I took him and his friends out to lunch.’ When her father read the story, he said: ‘Yes, Miss Ellah, it’s very good.’ But he was a traditional writer; he believed stories should have a beginning, middle and end, and a moral lesson. Hers didn’t have any of that. ‘The next month, he sent in a story and he won,’ Wakatama told me. ‘It’s something a therapist would have a field day with but, in our house, it was a massive joke.’

Pius Wakatama was a man of strong opinions and believed all his children should have opinions, too. He would argue with them and expect them to argue back. ‘Are you a man or a mouse?’ he once asked Nhamu, Ellah’s younger brother, when he refused to engage. ‘Dad, I’m a mouse,’ Nhamu responded. (Ellah laughed at the memory.) Pius was also extraordinarily large-hearted, often bringing home people who were in a tight spot: struggling relatives, street families, hitchhikers. ‘I grew up with that kind of thing,’ Wakatama said. ‘I think it had a profound effect on me … this idea that your life has to have meaning, that you can’t just exist, that you have to be impacting the world.’ Once, at the school where he taught, he heard a student crying in the girls’ bathroom because her parents wanted to marry her off. ‘Don’t worry,’ Pius told the young woman. ‘Bring your suitcase with you tomorrow.’ He went home and told Winnie he was bringing her a new daughter. The next day, he knocked on Ellah’s bedroom door and said: ‘This is Florence, she’s your sister.’

Wakatama went to the same college as her mother, a small Mennonite school in rural Indiana. There, in her final year, she declared that she would not read. Specifically – and ‘with all the irritating self-riotousness of youth,’ as she once put it – she announced that she would not be reading any dead white males. Craft your own reading list, her professor told her. This was a turning point. ‘Even though it would be years later that I started working as a publisher, it defined how I approached publishing,’ she told me. ‘The bookshelf was wrong; I knew there was more to it. My professor challenged me to find that “more” – and I did.’

She put James Baldwin on her list, and Alice Walker. Then she discovered Tsitsi Dangarembga.

Dangarembga’s Nervous Conditions (1988) was the first book published in English by a Black Zimbabwean woman. It follows 13-year-old Tambu at a mission school and confronts the ‘nervous conditions’ – a phrase taken from Jean-Paul Sartre – of being caught between traditional African culture and Western colonial influence. The novel’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – jolted Wakatama, not least because Tambu’s brother had almost the same name as Wakatama’s brother, Nhamu. It felt as if, in exploring the dissonance of social mobility in Zimbabwe, Dangarembga was writing about Wakatama and her peers: she ‘felt that the author had peeked inside our most secret diaries and written us into being.’

More than a decade would pass before Wakatama found her way back to books. After college, she married Richard Allfrey, a British boy she’d met in the US, and, while in grad school, decided to have a child because she was ‘curious about motherhood’. She wrote her dissertation with little Gabrielle on her lap. (‘I’d breastfeed and type, breastfeed and type.’) Afterwards, the family moved to England, where she worked a series of jobs in the education sector. ‘I hated every single one,’ she said. The racism in England rankled her but, more than that, she was bored. One day, on holiday in Zimbabwe, her parents sat her down. Pius asked what she was doing with her life. Her mother added: ‘You’ve been sitting on your brain so long you’re going to forget to use it.’

‘They didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out with the guys in the post room because they were Black’

Ellah cried after that intervention. She felt she was letting down her family, letting down Zimbabwe – in those early postcolonial years, the feeling was that your education was meant to improve things. Then her daughter unwittingly spearheaded another intervention. ‘We can’t live with you because you’re so unhappy,’ Gabrielle, seven at the time, told her after she returned from work one day. ‘You spend all your time and money on books,’ Richard chimed in. ‘Why don’t you just work in books?’

Gabrielle, now 34 years old, doesn’t remember giving her mother this advice, though she told me it must have been very good advice for a seven-year-old. She and her sister Rujeko, born 10 years after Gabrielle, were also in Accra. She was enjoying seeing her mother work with writers. Wakatama knew how to talk with writers in a way she hadn’t instinctively known how to talk to babies. When Gabrielle was born, Wakatama – unsure of how to interact with an infant – would read her the paper. This was the 1990s and the Soviet Union had crumbled, so she read Gabrielle stories about Boris Yeltsin. What Gabrielle remembers is struggling with dyslexia

and her mother encouraging her to read, being patient, open and supportive.

After that second intervention, Wakatama worked for a year as a temp at Penguin’s offices in London, before being hired as an assistant to both the editor of the Ancient Classics series and the editor of the Modern Classics series. She was 30. There were books everywhere, piles on the floor, spilling out of cabinets, teetering stacks on desks. I’m home, she thought to herself. But the trouble with being home is that sometimes not everyone there accepts that it is your home. ‘I knew I was with my tribe of people,’ she told me. ‘But they didn’t recognise me as a member of the tribe. I would hang out quite a bit with the guys in the post room because they were Black. Nobody was cruel to me – it just never occurred to them at the time.’

She paused. ‘I didn’t look like an editor because none of the editors looked like me.’

She’d sit at the desk looking at the Modern Classics: there were Russian writers, and Japanese writers, and French writers. She began to wonder where the African writers were. ‘How can you say you have a Modern Classics list, and you don’t have Achebe? You don’t have Ngũgĩ? It made absolutely no sense to me.’ Encouraged by her boss, she reached out to people who’d worked at the African Writers Series, and licensed some of those authors: Dambudzo Marechera from Zimbabwe, Bessie Head from Botswana, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o from Kenya. She became interested in Black writers from elsewhere, for instance championing the work of the Jamaican-born Linton Kwesi Johnson, who became the first Black poet, and the second living poet, to be included in the Penguin Modern Classics series.

‘I wasn’t at this point thinking I’m out to change literature,’ she told me. ‘I just thought this bookshelf is wrong. As a child of independence, you know you’re supposed to be changing the world, you don’t just submit and do your job. Plus, I was ambitious as fuck.’

It’s hard to write about editors. Who profiles editors? Writers are easier, at least published ones. Why did you say this 40 years ago, you might ask them; Why does the structure of your novel resemble Flaubert? While talking to Wakatama – we were discussing Wole Soyinka’s hair (‘like a cloud!’) and that time in 2010 she interviewed him – my own early obsessions returned to me: Peter Abrahams and the world of 1940s Johannesburg he created in Mine Boy (1946), Gustave Flaubert’s Parisian aristocrats in Sentimental Education (1869). I knew from an early age that I was going to be a writer; I’d been trapped by literature, deriving pleasure ever since from moments when I could do what those writers did: bring an idea in my head to life on the page, turn a half-formed thought or image into a sparkling sentence.

None of these moments would have been possible without an editor. Only a specific kind of obsessive understands Andy Elisburg’s role in the Miami Heat’s NBA championships, or Elvira Nabiullina’s in Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine, and it’s the same with editors. Writers know. Without an editor who ‘gets it’, we have little chance of succeeding – a sentence my editor most certainly did not force me to write. Or, think of musicians and their producers: there was no Michael Jackson without Berry Gordy, or Kendrick Lamar without Dr Dre. I mentioned Dre to Wakatama, specifically the way she stopped trying to be a poet and began publishing other writers, just as he killed his own rap career, and she cackled.

‘No one’s ever compared me to Dr Dre before!’

The books she is drawn to are ones ‘that feel like they had to be written’, she tells me later, when I ask about the bookshelf she is building, the one her grandchildren will refer to. ‘There has to be a message, a question, an exploration. This works best when filtered through character and place – so the story is equally important.’ In this, she has come to agree with Pius: a story needs a message and a plot. But she remains drawn to beauty. ‘It’s the layers underneath that will keep me reading and re-reading,’ she added. ‘I remain obsessed with beautiful sentences, that delicate crafting of the thought until it becomes poetry.’

Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done

After Penguin, Wakatama moved to Jonathan Cape, an imprint of Random House. Among the first big writers whose books she worked on were Julian Barnes and Ian McEwan. She said: ‘I copyedited On Chesil Beach, which has one mistake in it.’

I said I would read the book to try to find it.

She laughed and said: ‘You won’t know the mistake. If you find it, tell me. Ian said it was his fault, not mine, but I still blame myself.’

Although she now had more room to commission books, her acquisitions budget was still tiny. She scoured the list of writers awarded grants by the Arts Council of England, reaching out to them to see if they had anything to publish. That’s how she published Biyi Bandele’s Burma Boy (2007), about African soldiers in the Second World War, and Nii Ayikwei Parkes’s debut novel Tail of the Blue Bird (2009), a thriller that blends forensic science and Ghanaian folklore. Both challenged the way she thought about editing. In a multi-lingual book, for instance, the non-English parts are usually italicised. But Ayikwei Parkes refused to submit to this; in Blue Bird, this convention is flipped. Typically, ‘English is the standard and the rest of us are deviations,’ she told me. But in Blue Bird, a lot of the narration is by a man who doesn’t speak English: only when he uses a non-Akan word (particular to English) do italics appear. Ayikwei Parkes’s insistence on italicising these individual words of English, rather than those of Twi or Ga, was an assertion that the centre of the world was where the writer said it was, that Western readers should have to do the work that the African reader has always done.

‘That was really, for me, political,’ she said.

Ayikwei Parkes told me how unexpected it had been to find an editor willing to change her mind about editorial style. ‘For most conventional editors, it might be baffling to accommodate such a conceit,’ he said. ‘But she fully grasped the political thrust of my stylistic choice and supported its use, protecting me from the clutches of standard copyeditors.’ When I mentioned the Achebe-Wakatama comparison to him, he disagreed. ‘I sort of resist the idea of godparents for African writing, a notion that doesn’t exist for Western writing. What I will say is that Ellah is, like Achebe, certainly interested in the dignity and autonomy of the African personality and perspective. She believes and understands that Africa is a continent from which the world can be observed, made sense of, influenced and remade.’

Growing up in Zimbabwe, Wakatama says, made her a better editor. ‘Because as an African, for my generation at least, you grow up in an education system that doesn’t include you in the literature; therefore, you have to fill in the gaps yourself. So almost any African, if they were a reader anyway, is going to be a better reader than an English person – because we’re always reading outside ourselves, as well as within ourselves.’ She paused. ‘Which I don’t think we acknowledge enough. I think, now that I’m older, especially post-menopause, and also senior enough not to care what anyone thinks, I can just say it out loud.’

It has taken decades of being dismissed for her to speak so freely: of working under bosses who paid lip-service to diversity, of going to award ceremonies and realising the only other Black people in the room were waiters, of having smaller purchasing and marketing budgets than her colleagues. She recalls trying to acquire a book once, championing it fiercely, but being turned down – mere months later, it was bought by another editor in a different division for five times the price. ‘I told them: This is nonsense – you could have had this book for five grand six months ago when I found it, but because someone else says that it’s good, you’re now going to take it. What the fuck?’

Above her desk at Random House, she’d put up a picture of Toni Morrison, previously an editor at the company. ‘I used to look at that picture and think: She survived and I can too.’ But it was after the death of Nhamu, her younger brother, that she decided things could not go on as they had. Nhamu had suffered a series of strokes, and his death a decade later catapulted Wakatama into a deep depression, a depression that would be matched in depth only by the one triggered by her later divorce from her husband. ‘[Nhamu] was one of the true loves of my life,’ she told me, dabbing her eyes. ‘I was a completely different person after he died … his dying made me think: If he’s gone and I’m left behind – if his life has ended, what am I gonna do with mine?’

‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long’

Shortly after, she joined Granta as deputy editor of the literary magazine. She loved its international scope and finally had what she’d always wanted: a proper budget for commissioning writers. She also began to commission authors for Granta Books. She said: ‘I am driven by a mission, I really am. I’m not a religious person, but I grew up in a religious family. Part of that is about what are you here on earth for? The most important thing to me is books. My daughters will absolutely tell you that they had to fight for my attention. And I want others to have the chance to experience what I’ve experienced. Granta finally gave me that opportunity to do that level of commissioning.’

She started doing workshops – in Nigeria, China, Sri Lanka – to train other editors, as well as more public talks and radio. Her first big interview was with Wole Soyinka. She read him a poem on stage; it was a poem he had written when younger about what he’d be like when his hair was silver. Ellah told him: ‘Look at you now, you’re pretty much all silver. You know, what do you think about the poem?’ The great man laughed.

In 2011, she was awarded an Order of the British Empire for her services to the publishing industry. Somebody noticed, she thought to herself, somebody noticed the work I’m doing. Meanwhile, some colleagues asked: Well, what are you getting that for? ‘We now call these microaggressions, which are never microaggressions,’ she said. ‘My answer was always, for surviving this.’

What does it mean to be the only person of your kind in a room, constantly having to prove you belong? For Wakatama, the cost was psychological. ‘I wish someone had said to me: This life that you’re living is really fulfilling your soul but beware of the damage it will do to you,’ she said. It is tempting to buy into the hoopla of being the first this-or-that, of having a seat at the table, ‘to get sucked into that sense of, Oh, I’m special,’ she warns. ‘My feeling is that, if I am sitting at that table, to not sit at that table for too long.’

Part of her mission, therefore, is to continue to facilitate the entry of gifted writers into the global publishing infrastructure. In this regard, the English writer Max Porter, who worked alongside Wakatama at Granta, describes her as ‘a proper writer’s editor, deeply committed to and connected to her writers, not necessarily just the one book she is working on.’ As someone new at the time to the publishing world and ‘a little suspicious of it already’, Porter was inspired by how Wakatama nurtured and protected the writers she worked with ‘in the line and on the page and in the world.’

In 2020, after the murder of George Floyd forced a new racial reckoning in the United States and beyond, Wakatama watched white agents rush to sign Black writers. ‘I was like, you’ve got to be kidding me,’ she recalled. ‘After 20 years of saying: Publish Black writers now, you have this.’ Young writers were suddenly being offered massive advances. ‘On one level, that’s great – I’m thinking: Baby, take the money and run! But when you pay half a million for a book and the book sells 10,000 copies, it’s a failure. Remember, it’s an advance against your royalties. So, the next time, you’re starting off in debt.’ The result is that the publisher thinks these books don’t sell and ‘you’ve made it impossible for those authors to be successful.’

In Accra, I sat in on some of the Pfumo sessions. One reason Wakatama co-founded the collective was her concern about how few African nonfiction writers were published internationally. As the participants discussed writing craft, she listened closely, her head tilted towards the speaker, her legs crossed. When she talked, she leaned back, her hands a vital part of her speech. Books surrounded us. (‘It’s overwhelming to realise how many of these I edited,’ she told me.)

When a participant read out her work softly, Wakatama told her to read it again because she wanted ‘a big voice’. Here are other things she said to the writers presenting their work:

‘How do you feel about that?’
‘You’re not being brave enough. I need you to be brave.’
‘Greener pastures, no. That’s a cliché. We don’t use them.’
‘I don’t want you to run away. I want you to try. I think you’ll get it.’
‘I know I said lean into the poetry, but maybe you leaned too much.’

One evening in 2017, Wakatama saw a post on Facebook by Dangarembga, the author of Nervous Conditions. That book’s opening sentence – ‘I was not sorry when my brother died’ – had shocked Ellah, but when her own Nhamu died, she returned to the novel in her sorrow. How astutely Dangarembga had written of what Ellah herself had to grapple with: ‘the psychic trauma of fitting into a world that seems to demand an erasure, a forgetting of the self before.’ Dangarembga’s second novel, The Book of Not, had come out in 2006. She was now seeking an editor for her third, which she would self-publish.

That Dangarembga would struggle to find a publisher despite her success was an indictment of an industry that still struggled to recognise African writers. Wakatama didn’t know Dangarembga personally but she reached out anyway. ‘Your writing is so important to so many of us, why are you self-publishing?’ she asked. ‘If you do self-publish, please can I offer my services for free as your editor?’

The new book – This Mournable Body (2018) – was remarkable, Wakatama thought, and she offered to introduce Dangarembga to a friend who ran Graywolf Press, an American indie publisher. Wakatama flew to Harare; Dangarembga came to the family house for lunch. When she was younger, Dangarembga recalled, she often corresponded with a Zimbabwean writer called Pius Wakatama. Was he a relative, Dangarembga wondered. Pius laughed. It was him.

Graywolf bought the book. Wakatama was then still editing it for free, but she added a clause in the contract stipulating that the publisher would pay her an extra (hefty) fee if the book made it to the Booker shortlist. ‘Everyone was fine with it because it was never going to happen,’ she recalled, smiling. But by now Wakatama knew to bet on herself. ‘When she got shortlisted and the money hit my account, I was, like, Yeah. I told you all.’

item.title: A plane crossing the Moon
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
How a harmless thought turned into one man’s 10-year odyssey: to film a plane silhouetted against the Moon

- Directed by Agustín Ferrando Trenchi

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
English subtitles for this video are available by clicking the ‘Settings’ button on the bottom right of the video player.

In 2015, the Uruguayan filmmaker Agustín Ferrando Trenchi assigned himself a peculiar mission on a whim – he wanted to film a plane crossing in front of the Moon serendipitously, without planning for it. As he discusses in this short film, he quickly discovered how difficult a task that was. As the years went by, he captured many moments of ‘pure beauty’, including the various ways the Moon can manifest in the night sky, and striking shots of all manner of other objects silhouetted against it, but no plane. Narrating the footage he shot over 10 years, Ferrando Trenchi describes the learning and joy inherent to his task, even as finding just the right angle to complete his mission long eluded him, until – well, you’ll just have to watch to find out.

Via Kottke

item.title: On Japan’s Shinkansen trains, pork buns split reality in two
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Fujioka
item.description:
If eating on a public train gets seen as an act of terrorism, insights from olfactory genetics can pave the way for empathy

- by Yusuke Fujioka

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Each day, Japan’s high-speed Shinkansen rail network carries roughly half a million passengers between Osaka and Tokyo. Passengers begin their journey by boarding the train and, after finding their assigned seat, settling in. But, once the doors on the express trains close, there’s no stepping off again until they have reached their final stop – whether that’s two hours away or five.

Within this mobile confinement, ‘pork bun terrorism’ periodically erupts. The ‘attack’ begins innocently: a passenger purchases a steaming-hot pork bun at Shin-Osaka station, for example, anticipating the modest pleasure of consuming it during the journey. Yet, once the package is opened and the passenger begins to eat, the smell of steamed dough, onion and hot pork fat spreads through the surrounding rows. A swift – and sometimes vociferous – rebuke from a nearby passenger may follow. Sometimes, the exchange may escalate into a heated altercation.

The controversy first drew widespread attention online in 2018 and has resurfaced periodically ever since. Despite being asked to adjudicate on the matter, the railway companies that operate Japan’s Shinkansen trains have largely avoided a blanket ban on strong-smelling food, relying instead on passengers’ discretion and consideration for others. But the issue keeps flaring up.

The question of whether pork buns should be eaten aboard Shinkansen trains has sharply polarised opinion into two seemingly irreconcilable camps. On one side are the passengers who feel entitled to eat what they like on board (especially when it involves food they see as harmless), and on the other side are those who consider the unwanted smell of pork buns to be an inescapable imposition. What makes the dispute unusually combustible is that both sides regard their own experience as self-evident. Each interprets the other’s reaction as rude or unreasonable.

I find myself siding with those who oppose eating pork buns on the Shinkansen. The smell causes me intense, visceral discomfort. I have long struggled to understand how anyone could introduce such a pervasive odour into a confined space where others cannot escape it.

He regarded the complaint as an attempt by a stranger to impose a personal standard on him

By contrast, those who defend the eating of pork buns appear entirely bewildered by this response. They argue that they are merely enjoying a delicious local delicacy sold at the station and cannot understand why they are met with what they regard as misplaced anger, from critics who seem intolerant and hypersensitive.

In 2026, another case of ‘pork-bun terrorism’ made these positions particularly vivid. A Japanese entrepreneur posted online that a fellow passenger aboard the Shinkansen had reprimanded him for eating a pork bun – one of the much-loved 551 Horai pork buns sold at Shin-Osaka Station. He regarded the complaint as an attempt by a stranger to impose a personal standard on him: eating was permitted onboard, he argued, and the buns were sold hot at Shin-Osaka Station. To him, eating a pork bun was an ordinary pleasure of travel. Debate erupted once again.

Although Japan is widely known for its exacting norms of public etiquette, the pork bun problem remains an anomaly, resisting resolution through conventional appeals to manners. Why, on this particular issue, are we so incapable of understanding one another?

Research suggests that the answer has less to do with tolerance than with the fact that each side is, quite literally, experiencing a different reality.

As a neurologist who studies the brain and sensory perception, I have arrived at a specific hypothesis. A profound misconception lies at the root of this conflict. The misconception is this: because we occupy the same physical space and are exposed to the same odours, we assume that the person next to us perceives them exactly as we do. More generally, we mistake shared space for shared perception. Viewed through this lens, the structure of the pork bun conflict becomes clearer.

If we define manners as the voluntary modification of one’s behaviour out of consideration for others, then the premise of broadly shared perception often serves as a practical foundation for etiquette. When we assume that our internal experience roughly aligns with that of others, we can more readily imagine their feelings and adjust our conduct accordingly. For instance, when we wait our turn in a crowded queue, we assume that others, too, would be inconvenienced by queue-jumping. When we refrain from littering, we assume others would find a litter-strewn path unpleasant. This presumed alignment allows us to act considerately without being asked.

An intractable problem arises when what appears to be a shared experience has unknowingly fractured beneath the surface

However, we can encounter situations in daily life where this premise does not hold. Consider when someone offers their train seat to an elderly person or a pregnant woman. The person offering up their seat doesn’t need to be elderly or pregnant to respond considerately. They don’t need to share the same immediate experience to act because the other person’s physical difficulty is readily apparent and easy to imagine. That means that, even when the burdens experienced by two people are starkly different, mutual courtesy can bridge the gap, as long as both people understand the nature of that difference.

This premise works, mostly. However, an intractable problem arises when what appears to be a shared experience has unknowingly fractured beneath the surface. In such cases, conventional manners alone may be insufficient to resolve the conflict. That makes the pork bun problem an unusually demanding test of social etiquette.

So how, exactly, does this premise of shared experience break down inside a Shinkansen carriage?

Differences in our genes can shape how we perceive smells. The best-known example of this phenomenon involves the plant Coriandrum sativum (known as coriander or cilantro). While some individuals relish it as a refreshing herb, others find it deeply unpleasant, perceiving an odour reminiscent of soap or stink bugs. This divergence has been linked to a genetic variant near OR6A2, a gene involved in detecting smells. Such variation may affect the perceived intensity of the plant’s scent and also odour quality. The same leaves can seem fresh and herbaceous to one person but soapy or bug-like to another.

The pork bun controversy seems to reflect a similar form of olfactory diversity. It is known that pork fat can contain a volatile steroid compound called androstenone, which contributes to what is often characterised as an animal-like odour. Intriguingly, how people perceive this compound is strongly associated with variation in the olfactory receptor gene OR7D4. People inherit two copies of this particular smell-related gene, one from each parent. But those who happen to have inherited the more ‘sensitive’ versions of both copies tend to have a much lower threshold for detecting androstenone. For them, even a small trace of this compound is likely to be perceived as an unpleasant or animal-like odour.

Those who experience the smell of pork buns as something pleasant are not necessarily inconsiderate

Conversely, research from 2012 by Kathrine Lunde of the Norwegian Meat Research Centre and colleagues shows that people carrying different gene variants tend to perceive androstenone as less intense and less unpleasant. Over the course of primate evolution, vision became increasingly prominent, while smell mattered less. Eventually, many smell-related genes accumulated mutations and ‘switched off’. So how does this relate to ‘pork bun terrorism’?

Those who experience the smell of pork buns as something pleasant are not necessarily inconsiderate. Genetic studies suggest they may simply experience its aroma differently. To be clear, I am not claiming that androstenone alone accounts for the animal-like odour of pork buns. Nevertheless, the association between variation in the OR7D4 gene and androstenone perception offers a useful conceptual model for understanding the structure of the pork bun dispute on Japan’s Shinkansen.

If genetic variation in our smell receptors can alter how odours are perceived, then the foundational assumption that people in the same space experience the same odour in the same way is false. Furthermore, these genetic differences are mostly invisible and unknown to those who are (or are not) concerned about the smell of pork buns. Exposed to the same food odour, one passenger may experience an unpleasant, animal-like smell that triggers an involuntary emotional response, while another perceives an appetising aroma. Neither party is exaggerating. Instead, their brains are constructing qualitatively different perceptual experiences from the same source.

In everyday life, one person may bear a disproportionate sensory burden that others do not recognise. Noise disputes offer a clear parallel: for a person with misophonia, a disorder in which certain sounds may lead to a disproportionate emotional reaction, merely hearing someone chewing or breathing may provoke intense, involuntary distress. If we assume that everyone experiences the same sound in the same way, that distress – and any request for relief – may seem incomprehensible. Similarly, disputes over office thermostat settings often become intractable because we too readily assume that the same room temperature produces the same bodily experience in everyone.

Another problem is that, in each case, the less-affected person often decides what counts as a reasonable reaction. If the stimulus seems tolerable to them, they assume that it should be tolerable to everyone. The person who is more affected is then dismissed as overreacting, even though the burden is not equally shared.

Following this logic, it becomes clear that such conflicts cannot be adequately resolved by rigid rules, nor by demanding equal concessions from both sides.

Hidden biological differences may be undermining the assumptions that make social cooperation possible. Equipped with scientific knowledge, we have a responsibility to explain these hidden asymmetries so that we can comprehend each other’s lived realities. Scientific understanding does not automatically make people kinder, but it can show us where empathy is needed.

If people could genuinely imagine the profound distress their actions might cause, more passengers might voluntarily refrain from eating pork buns on the Shinkansen. At the same time, those who find the odour repulsive might come to see that their ability to travel in an environment free of strong food odours is partly sustained by other passengers’ restraint. That recognition might foster gratitude toward those who choose to forgo a small pleasure during the journey. Demands can then become requests, and restraint can be recognised as an act of consideration.

Some people will undoubtedly continue to prioritise their own pleasure even when they understand another person’s distress. However, once invisible burdens are made comprehensible, the conflict need no longer be reduced to a petty squabble between people labelled ‘hypersensitive’ and ‘insensitive’. Only then can the real work begin: making requests, showing consideration, expressing gratitude and, where necessary, designing appropriate rules and environments.

The next time ‘pork bun terrorism’ erupts on a Shinkansen, perhaps there will be a pause before the first bite or the first rebuke. Could etiquette begin in that pause, as two Shinkansen passengers realise that the same pork bun may be taking their noses on very different journeys?

item.title: Everyone says they have anxiety. Clinical anxiety is different
item.dc:creator: India Sturgis
item.description:
Anxiety put me in hospital. I’ve learned you can’t eradicate what is part of you – but you can change how you relate to it

- by India Sturgis

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
You’ve probably noticed that terms once used only within the confines of a therapist’s office are now deployed unthinkingly to describe experiences that are merely uncomfortable. A car backfires and someone says it has ‘given them anxiety’. Spilling a round of drinks in front of others results in ‘PTSD’ – or ‘OCD’ until they are cleared up. On TikTok, I’ve seen someone’s ‘ponytail era’ or syrup stains on a hardwood floor being described as severely traumatic. Likewise, the everyday use of language that surrounds anxiety conditions – words like ‘worry’, ‘fear’, ‘rumination’, ‘panic’, and ‘anxiety’ itself – makes it easy to underestimate just how debilitating anxiety-related illnesses can be.

As a journalist, I’ve spent years interviewing experts and people living with anxiety for my book How to Eat an Elephant (2026). I also have my own personal experience with anxiety. In 2019, I was diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder (GAD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and chronic insomnia, which I have since rowed back from, over months and years. My hope is for more people to recognise just how serious anxiety can become, not least so they know when to get the help they need – but also to appreciate that it’s an essential, unavoidable part of life.

It’s normal to feel anxiety during challenging life moments or periods of intense change. To sweep mild and transient issues into the language of disorder helps no one, and particularly not those who really are struggling with mental ill health. Nerves help us make decisions quickly, weigh up risk, and compete at the top of our game. The professional golfer Tiger Woods put it well in an interview in 2015: ‘I care about what I do and when I’m not nervous is the day I quit … I want to feel the rush, I want to feel the nerves.’

So we need some anxiety in our lives, but we also need to know when it has outstayed its welcome or grown to unhelpful and life-altering proportions. Anxiety conditions are the most common form of mental illness, affecting a third of us in our lifetime, according to best estimates. Data from the NHS in England suggest that 7.5 per cent of adults are currently living with GAD, the most common anxiety disorder. Despite this, global data show that only one in four people with an anxiety disorder will receive any form of treatment for it, which is particularly frustrating given how highly treatable anxiety is.

The consultant psychologist Elena Touroni says confusion around anxiety creeps in because we use it to describe such a wide spectrum of experience: ‘It’s used for both the nerves before a presentation, and the experience of someone whose anxiety is shaping every decision they make, narrowing their world and affecting their sleep, their relationships and their ability to function.’

According to Touroni, it’s not surprising that people struggle to locate themselves on that spectrum, or to recognise when what they are experiencing has crossed into something that warrants proper support. ‘The line between normal and clinical is not obvious and can feel quite subjective to people who don’t have specialist support,’ she says. ‘I regularly work with people who have been managing a significant level of anxiety for years without recognising it as anything other than just how they are. They have adapted to it and it has become their baseline.’

Doctors typically look at how significantly symptoms interfere with your ability to function day to day

This resonates with me. Before I ended up in a psychiatric hospital in 2019, I had spent seven years struggling on and off with insomnia and anxiety to varying degrees. I sought concerted help only right at the end, when I was going multiple nights a week with just three or so hours of sleep – sometimes spending whole nights awake – utterly unable to switch off and, by then, having intrusive thoughts about suicide and self-harm. It sounds dramatic now – and it was – but it felt easier at the time to try to carry on and pretend nothing was wrong, hopeful things would get better on their own, particularly given I knew so little about anxiety.

So how do experts make a diagnosis of clinical anxiety? In the absence of a failsafe test, doctors typically look at how long you’ve had symptoms, their severity, and how significantly they interfere with your ability to function day to day.

‘What distinguishes a clinical anxiety disorder is not the presence of anxious thoughts, jitters or that horrible knot in the pit of your stomach,’ says Touroni, ‘but what happens to them over time. In clinical anxiety, the symptoms are more intense and persistent and, crucially, they do not lift once the perceived threat has gone. The nervous system either stays in a state of high alert long after the trigger has passed, or it begins firing in the absence of any clear trigger at all. Clinically, if someone has been experiencing this for six months or more, we would look seriously at whether they are dealing with an anxiety disorder.’

I knew things were escalating when I kept getting ill (my immune system was having a hard time with the insomnia), my mood had plummeted, and I started having panic attacks at night. I was anxious about feeling anxious and not sleeping. Everything was compounding and, as a result, I wanted to go out less.

Touroni explains that many people go for years carrying the physical and emotional toll of managing an anxiety disorder. This is a shame as ‘anxiety disorders are among the most treatable conditions we see in psychological practice.’ She adds: ‘Getting the right name for something is not a small thing, as it changes what feels possible and can have a huge impact on a person’s quality of life.’

Now – seven years after being hospitalised – I’m pleased to say anxiety is not a defining feature of my life, it’s just another brick in the wall of my personality. What helped me most when I was in crisis was being taken out of my home environment for a couple of weeks, medication (sertraline, an SSRI antidepressant, in the mornings and amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant that can help with sleep, in the evenings), cognitive behavioural therapy, and learning how anxiety as a pathological illness functions in the mind and body.

I know I have a tendency towards anxiety, but I also now know what helps me steer away from it in pressing moments: prioritising sleep, work-life balance, managing stress, eating well, saying ‘no’ and being self-compassionate, among other things.

It’s my tendency towards anxiety that makes me so enjoy life. I am quick to think and feel

The psychologist and researcher Nick Grey puts it like this: ‘Can we cure anxiety? No, because it’s part of the human condition. If someone’s goal is I never want to feel anxious again, then no, that won’t happen. But if the goal is about overcoming a chronic anxiety problem in which the person is stuck, then absolutely, that can happen. You can’t get rid of anxiety, but you can absolutely overcome chronic anxiety problems.’

The psychologist Rollo May was of a similar opinion. I like what he wrote in The Meaning of Anxiety (rev ed, 1977):

Anxiety cannot be avoided, but it can be reduced. The problem of the management of anxiety is that of reducing the anxiety to normal levels, and then to use this normal anxiety as stimulation to increase one’s awareness, vigilance, zest for living.

True to his perspective, I’ve come to see that it’s my tendency towards anxiety that makes me so enjoy life. I am quick to think and feel. And while I now recognise the need to pay better attention to anxiety when I feel it – weighing up what my mind and body are trying to tell me rather than pretending it doesn’t exist and pushing the sensation away – I wouldn’t change my underlying sensitive nature for anything.

If reading this has made you reflect on whether you’ve been living with problematic anxiety, it may help to have a sense of how long it could take to learn to manage it better. It could be months or years, depending on what the issue is and how long it has existed. Not days. In many cases, not even weeks. Too often, we put pressure on ourselves to ‘get better’ immediately once we realise we are sick or struggling. Grey says: ‘People assume if things haven’t changed quickly enough, then there’s no hope. But recovery is an up and down rollercoaster route. There’s always hope, even if you’ve had an anxiety problem for decades.’

Anxiety, then, is not always the enemy, but we should treat it with respect. That’s why our relationship to it matters: so we can recognise and meet it when it spills into something pathological.

item.title: Can you ever really think what someone else is thinking?
item.dc:creator: Víctor Verdejo
item.description:
To see how communication truly works, we should set aside the notion that different people can share the same thoughts

- by Víctor Verdejo

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Most of us have had the experience of looking into someone’s eyes and sensing that we know what’s on their mind. Not much is needed for this sense of knowing what someone is thinking: some words, a gesture, a smile, or just a shared gaze. Friends exchange comments about their day and nod affirmatively. Parents utter ‘Oh my God’ as they watch their toddler take a first step. Commuters give each other a weary glance as the train pulls away without them. Encounters like these involve a meeting of minds – we feel that we understand and are understood.

Having the opportunity to connect with others in this way is gratifying. It provides a sense of belonging to a wider sphere, a sphere where your thoughts and your meanings are not just your thoughts and your meanings. Where they are open to another. When communication unfolds successfully – when the click happens, or insofar as the click happens – you and another person can seem to be thinking the same thing.

This idea transpires in the way people talk: we tend to speak as if we literally share thoughts, as though ideas can flow seamlessly from one mind to another. We often say that we ‘think the same’ or ‘know what’s on somebody’s mind’ or ‘get our thoughts across’. These are natural illustrations of how much people unreflectively rely on the idea that thoughts are not only shareable but indeed are ordinarily shared in our communicative exchanges.

This intuitive picture is old and powerful. Yet the notion that people think the very same thought in successful communication has come under increasing scrutiny. Contemporary philosophers argue that what seems like straightforward thought-sharing is more complex, and more interesting, than the familiar metaphors suggest. They both challenge this natural idea and show that understanding each other plausibly involves thinking differently from each other. Realising this can help us see how communication really works.

The idea that communication and understanding are built on shared thoughts has a long history. Plato influentially suggested that ideas involved in our knowledge and talk are in fact unchanging, perfect forms inhabiting a separate realm – a shared eidetic foundation of reality. Augustine of Hippo, in De doctrina Christiana (397-426), expressed the view that signs are used to ‘transmit to another’s mind what is in the mind of the person who gives the sign’. But the basic schema that informs our communicative intuitions nowadays was more clearly proclaimed in the modern period. In the third book of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), John Locke contended that the purpose of communication via language is the transfer of thoughts or ideas from one person to another:

The chief end of language in communication being to be understood, words serve not well for that end, neither in civil nor philosophical discourse, when any word does not excite in the hearer the same idea which it stands for in the mind of the speaker.

This view persisted from the 19th century to the present, in the work of philosophical giants such as Gottlob Frege, H P Grice and Robert Stalnaker, among others. Frege, for instance, advocated a conception of shareable thoughts that result in a ‘common stock’ consistent with logic and science. Stalnaker developed an influential framework for communicative contexts resting on the notion of a ‘common ground’, or information shared by the speakers in a conversation.

Whereas these and other works clearly align with the idea of thought-sharing, recent developments in thinking about the nature of communication suggest a more nuanced picture. Sometimes, of course, people suffer dramatic misalignment and just miscommunicate; the thought doesn’t get across, and they don’t understand each other. But even when communication succeeds in practical terms, there is often diversity and mismatch in what we’re thinking.

Effective communication is consistent with – and may even require – differences in thought

Suppose that, after a hard day’s work, you tell me, irascibly: ‘I had an awful day at work,’ to which I respond:, ‘I see.’ Here, there is a sense in which I perfectly understand what you said. But there are two ways in which this falls short of thought-sharing in the common sense of the term. First, your thought might be extremely rich – filled with feelings of frustration and details of the whole lot of things that have gone wrong throughout the day. But communication, in this case, doesn’t require us to share all of that. Moreover, even if you were to tell me all the ins and outs, there is some quality of the thought that can hardly be shared: after all, it is your job and your frustration. Even if I sympathise, it can barely affect me and my behaviour in the same way it affects yours.

People rarely, if ever, communicate about things as if from nowhere. Each of us must occupy a distinctive space, a point of view, with our own background knowledge, memories and current experience regarding the matters we talk about. A popular example from John Perry illustrates this cleanly: suppose that you are in the mountains with a hiking partner, and a bear starts to approach them. In fright, they shout: ‘A bear is about to attack me!’ You understand that they are in danger, so you run to get help while your partner defensively curls up into a ball. But if you completely shared your partner’s thought – which would include thought content about an imminent threat to the self, from their perspective – then you would behave in the same way that they do and curl up too.

In this case, as well as in more ordinary cases, effective communication is consistent with – and may even require – differences in thought. Our cognitive lives are, after all, so different. Our beliefs, backgrounds and sensibilities influence the specific content of our thoughts, and they can never really be the same from one thinker to the next.

In the science-fiction trope of the ‘hive mind’ (eg, the Borg of Star Trek, or the virus-induced collective consciousness of the 2025 TV show Pluribus), individual minds in the hive share all thoughts automatically and seamlessly; they are literally of one mind in every respect. If real-life communication consists of thought-sharing, it certainly isn’t like this for us, yet we sometimes talk as if it is. Recognising this is important: it not only avoids a distorted conception of communication, it also helps to calibrate our expectations when we communicate.

In recent philosophical work, there are some who defend a sophisticated version of thought-sharing. They make room for the variability of what people are actually thinking when they understand each other, but retain the idea that you can, in some sense, share a thought. This approach, which I myself favour, reflects that the basic concept of thought-sharing is not only natural, but explanatorily useful. For example, the notion that you can share a thought makes it easy to distinguish between misunderstanding what someone means (‘getting the wrong idea’) from grasping what someone means (‘getting the idea’) and yet disagreeing with it.

In this way of viewing thought-sharing, each person’s version of the shared thought is layered: thought similarity at one level is compatible with a level of disparity that reflects each person’s distinctive points of view. To constitute a ‘shared thought’, some core content or state must be identical, even as some other components of the thought differ. On this view, sharing thoughts is complex because thoughts themselves are complex.

Treating our thoughts as if they are about the same things often suffices for understanding and joint behaviour

But other philosophers explain communication differently: via coordination or informational relations among different thoughts. On these accounts, if I know or somehow track what you are thinking, I don’t actually need to ‘share’ your thought in order to understand what you are saying.

One particularly influential example of this is relationism, the kind of approach originally championed by Kit Fine. According to this perspective, communication is not really a matter of thought identity, but thought coordination. What matters is not the intrinsic properties of two people’s thoughts or the extent to which those are the same. What matters is how those thoughts are related. For instance, treating our thoughts as if they are about the same things often suffices for understanding and joint behaviour. So, if you tell me about your ‘awful day at work’, and elaborate about impending deadlines, an unkind boss and feeling overwhelmed, and I respond sympathetically, we both presuppose or act as if our thoughts are about these same things – even if the thoughts themselves are different – and doing so allows the conversation to serve its function. I may not need to share your experience in order to understand you. It might be enough that our thoughts coordinate – that they stand in an appropriate relation to one another.

The debate continues between proponents of these perspectives. But the richer picture drawn by these trends helps us think about communication and shared understanding without positing (as some would be tempted to) perfect matching in the way people think.

Let us return to our opening thought: the existence of mutual understanding, possibly triggered by words, gestures or even a simple glance. This prospect underwrites the possibility of a common world, and takes us beyond our private experiences. Yet recalcitrant, multifaceted difference is also an undeniable part of the picture. We should not expect mutual understanding in communication necessarily to lead to a common, monolithic thought or experience.

Noting this could prevent unnecessary frustration and overoptimistic expectations when we communicate. Communicating smoothly does bring our thoughts into contact with those of others. But there are important limits on someone else’s access to the full richness of your thoughts and point of view, and vice versa. Knowing this before we speak might inspire more patience in communication, more willingness to restate or elaborate in order to build the shared kernel of our differing thoughts, or a degree of acceptance when someone doesn’t seem to fully ‘get it’. It takes time and effort to share anything more than superficial or abstract thoughts and, even then, it is impossible to share everything we think. But that is exactly as it should be.

It may still seem plausible and useful to suppose that we can think ‘the same thing’. But, often, the connection you have to someone else’s thought is looser than it might appear, and interestingly complex. Whatever perspective you take, the question of whether or how we ever truly ‘share’ thoughts gives us reason to pause and consider what it actually means to connect with someone else – to understand and to be understood.

item.title: How to live a life of awe
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
You don’t need to climb Kilimanjaro or see the Northern Lights to experience the benefits of awe. It’s everywhere if you look

- Video by the University of California and the Greater Good Science Center

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Awe is that transcendent feeling of stepping out of the quotidian and encountering something vast, mysterious and beyond your comprehension. The experience is a human universal, deeply rooted in our evolutionary history to make us feel connected to the world beyond us. And, as Dacher Keltner, distinguished professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, explores in this video, you don’t need to summit Mount Kilimanjaro, or head to the Arctic to see the Northern Lights, to enjoy its myriad rewards. Rather, awe is all around us, if you know where to look. Borrowing from ideas in his book Awe: The New Science of Everyday Wonder and How It Can Transform Your Life (2023), Keltner details how awe works, why it benefits us and how we can feel more of it in our everyday lives.

For more on how to find awe in your daily life, read this Psyche Guide.

item.title: Why romantic relationships matter more to men than to women
item.dc:creator: Iris Wahring
item.description:
For too long, men were told to be self-sufficient. The research shows they’re more likely to thrive in a loving couple

- by Iris Wahring

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
For centuries, the self-sufficient man who shuns romance has appeared as a kind of noble figure. ‘He that hath wife and children hath given hostages to fortune,’ wrote Francis Bacon in ‘Of Marriage and the Single Life’ (1625). ‘Certainly the best works, and of greatest merit for the public, have proceeded from the unmarried or childless men.’ For Bacon, romantic relationships (and family) are impediments to a man becoming his best. Ralph Waldo Emerson devoted an entire essay, ‘Self-Reliance’ (1841), to the conviction that a man should stand apart from the crowd. ‘I shun father and mother and wife and brother, when my genius calls me,’ he wrote. Decades later, Rudyard Kipling reduced the idea to a single line: ‘He travels the fastest who travels alone.’

Such visions of self-sufficient masculinity endure in depictions of silent cowboys, wandering rōnin, desert hermits, elite soldiers, or libertines who treat love as a sport. Powered by their own strength and resilience, these men are domesticated only when circumstances or a determined partner finally insists on it. According to this view of masculinity, love is a welcome addition but never a need.

Women, on the other hand, have often been portrayed as being consumed by their desire for romantic relationships. Consider an often-quoted line from Lord Byron’s epic poem Don Juan (1819-24): love is just one part of a man’s life, Byron writes, but ‘tis woman’s whole existence’. If men can take or leave romance, the logic goes, then women must be the real romantics. They are the ones who fall harder and faster, and the ones who carry the emotional weight of a relationship.

But that’s not how things really work. As a researcher specialising in the psychology of romantic relationships, I have found that the evidence points the other way. In 2023 and 2024, I analysed more than 50 empirical studies and meta-analyses, revealing masculinity to be much more fragile than assumed. At every stage, from the first spark of attraction to the aftermath of a breakup, it is men who depend more on their romantic partners, for their happiness and, in measurable ways, for their survival.

To understand the disproportionate weight love carries for men, we must examine the trajectory of relationships, starting from the time when men are single and searching for a partner. On average, men consider finding a partner more important for their happiness than women do. When single, they are less satisfied with their relationship status and long for a partner more intensely. They also plunge into the feeling of falling in love more often and more quickly, and they experience unrequited love more frequently. Contrary to common expectations, men are typically the first to say ‘I love you’ in heterosexual relationships, according to a 2022 study led by Christopher Watkins from Abertay University in the UK, which surveyed participants across seven countries on three continents.

Once in a relationship, both partners usually benefit. Longitudinal research indicates that entering a romantic relationship itself is typically accompanied by increases in life satisfaction. Accordingly, couples tend to show higher levels of wellbeing, better mental and physical health, and even higher life expectancy than their single counterparts. Yet, all these benefits are more pronounced for men. For example, a 2020 meta-analysis by Yafeng Wang from Wuhan University in China and colleagues, involving data on marital status and mortality risk from 7.9 million individuals and 1.9 million deaths, found that unmarried women had a 22 per cent higher mortality risk than married women, but unmarried men even had a 46 per cent higher mortality risk than married men. So for the average man, being in a committed relationship is more decisive for how long they will live than it is for the average woman.

Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men

Many romantic relationships, however, end in a breakup and, if they do, this is typically initiated by women: among heterosexual couples, 60 to 70 per cent of breakups and divorces are initiated by women, according to studies in the US, Germany and Netherlands. The remaining 30 to 40 per cent are equally divided between mutual breakups and those initiated by men.

When the split happens, men suffer more. While a breakup is typically painful for women too, men tend to struggle more to find any positive aspects, such as relief or newfound independence, following a split. They are less likely to feel like they have learned something from the breakup. Men also tend to experience a sharper decline in life satisfaction, reporting higher levels of loneliness afterward and more frequently resorting to harmful coping mechanisms, such as alcohol and substance abuse.

Most alarmingly, the end of a relationship can be fatal. Following a divorce, the risk of suicide doubles for men. In a research paper in 2025, the men’s health expert Michael Wilson from the University of Melbourne and colleagues reviewed 75 prior studies on suicidality in men to find ‘the factors underpinning men’s suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, and death by suicide following relationship breakdown’. They found that the risk of suicide was especially high during the separation period itself, nearly twice the odds seen in men who were already divorced (and more than four times as high as married men). For women, the suicide risk after a divorce or separation increases by a far smaller amount, if at all. For a significant number of men, losing a romantic relationship is, quite literally, a matter of life or death.

How did we arrive at a place where the supposedly ‘stronger’ gender longs intensely for a partner, relies more heavily on them for health and wellbeing, is more frequently left behind, and remains emotionally fragile in the face of heartbreak? Multiple factors may play a role here.

Consider, for instance, the unequal distribution of household chores.
